newsitem.title: FRANCE: France wraps up airliner bomb probe, targets Libya.
newsitem.headline: France wraps up airliner bomb probe, targets Libya.

text.p: France's top anti-terrorism judge will this week complete an investigation into the bombing of a French airliner over the Sahara in 1989, and urge that four Libyan officials be tried in absentia, civil plaintiffs said.

Seven years to the day after the downing of a French UTA airlines DC-10 over Niger, judge Jean-Louis Bruguiere will on Thursday brief families of the 170 victims in Paris, and show them the painstakingly reconstructed airliner.

Victims' representatives contrasted the way the French probe swiftly found the crash was no accident with the agonisingly slow search to find out what brought down TWA Flight 800 off Long Island in July, killing 230 people.

"Judge Bruguiere is going to give us an account of his July trip to Libya and he will announce the investigation is finished and passed on to public prosecutors," Francoise Rudetski, head of the victims' SOS Attentats association, told Reuters.
"He will also take those relatives and friends who wish it to see the reconstruction of the airliner at the military airport of Le Bourget (outside Paris)," she said.

Sources close to the investigation said Bruguiere was likely to recommend a trial in absentia for the four suspects whose arrest he has sought, including Abdallah Senoussi, a brother-in-law of Libya's Colonel Muammar Gaddafi identified as a senior intelligence official.
The other suspects are Abdallah Elazragh, a diplomat working in Brazzaville at the time, and alleged secret agents Ibrahim Naeli and Musbah Arbas.

The destruction of the DC-10, in which nationals of more than a dozen countries were killed, occurred at the height of tension between France and Libya over Chad, where the two countries' armies clashed repeatedly in the 1970s and 1980s.
After a first fruitless attempt to enter Libya aboard a French warship in 1992, Bruguiere got to Tripoli in July under armed escort and questioned some 40 people on the DC-10.
During the July 5-16 visit, the Libyan secret service handed him a U.S.-made Samsonite suitcase which was full of pentrite, the same kind of explosive used in the bombing.
Libyan officials told the judge it had been found in 1990 at the home of opponents of Gaddafi, but he was not convinced.
"It was identical to the suitcase used in the bombing. We know that because of the suitcase fragments we found in the Tenere desert," one investigation source said.
Aside from the suitcase, Bruguiere returned with other unspecified new evidence.

"We can't all help thinking about July's TWA crash," Rudetzki said. "For the UTA flight the terrorist link was very quickly established. The U.S. elections are probably interfering with the results of the TWA inquiry."

She said most of the families of the UTA victims had requested they see the reconstructed airliner "to help them come out of mourning. Seeing the place where a loved one died is psychologically important".
Investigators have recovered some 80 percent of the doomed plane, and have pinpointed to the square metre where the bomb went off in the forward cargo loading bay.

The U.N. Security Council imposed economic sanctions on Libya over its refusal to hand over suspects in the DC-10 blast and in the 1988 explosion of Pan Am flight 103 over Lockerbie, Scotland, which killed 270 people.
